The upcoming MacBook Ultra is never going to be cheap. It features a brand-new, slimmer design, equipped with an OLED and touchscreen display—even before factoring in price hikes driven by rising memory costs, the price is already steep. And a latest report indicates that manufacturing costs may be pushed even higher.

Apple has always liked to source components from multiple suppliers to maximize display reliability and give itself greater bargaining power for the best possible pricing. It had originally planned to continue this approach with the MacBook Ultra. However, according to supply chain insiders, Apple has decided to use only one display supplier……

Apple has three display partners across its product lineup: Samsung, LG, and BOE. Among them, BOE has so far only supplied screens for the company's lower-end products, while orders for higher-end screens are split between Samsung and LG.

The MacBook Ultra will feature the most sophisticated display ever fitted to an Apple product. Combining stacked OLED with a touchscreen and applying it to the larger sizes required for a laptop is no easy feat. According to a recent supply chain report, Apple has decided that these screens will be supplied exclusively by Samsung.

Korean media outlet The Elec reports that LG failed to meet Apple's required production volume.

Apple required the use of large substrates for mass production. Samsung Display responded with its 8.6-generation OLED production line, while LG Display was reportedly considering continuing to use its existing 6-generation line. Even a 6-generation line can produce OLED panels for laptops, but in terms of substrate efficiency and output, it cannot match the 8.6-generation line. Because initial production volume was too low, Apple ultimately chose Samsung Display as its sole supplier.

It appears that the limited volume LG can produce is unable to offset the additional logistical complexity of using two suppliers. Outsiders expect that the company will not be able to supply screens for this flagship MacBook before 2029.

This clearly gives Samsung a stronger bargaining position on panel pricing, which is expected to push up Apple's manufacturing costs. Apple is very likely to pass on these expenses to consumers, just as it has handled the more expensive memory costs.

Considering that the MacBook Ultra's price may be shockingly high, how likely are you to consider upgrading? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
